title: "Compare assessment hypotheses"
output: rmarkdown::html_document

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tinyAM)
source_files <- list.files(system.file("R", package = "tinyAM"),
  pattern = "[.](R|rdb|rdx)$", full.names = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", warning = TRUE,
  cache.extra = list(package = as.character(packageVersion("tinyAM")),
    R = as.character(getRversion()), RTMB = as.character(packageVersion("RTMB")),
    mgcv = as.character(packageVersion("mgcv")),
    sources = unname(tools::md5sum(source_files)),
    inputs = cod_obs))
```

An age-structured assessment combines catch, survey indices and biology to
estimate abundance, recruitment and mortality. Different assumptions can explain
the same observations differently. This guide uses the Northern cod example to
compare three hypotheses, then inspect their diagnostics and forecasting skill.

The models match the [cheatsheet](../cheatsheet/tinyAM_cheatsheet.pdf). They are
SCAA-, SAM- and NCAM-*like* examples, rather than reproductions of complete
official assessments or recommended settings for another stock. For fleet catches
and multiple surveys, continue with [the simulated example](multiple-fisheries-surveys.html).

## Start with tidy inputs

```{r inputs}
dat <- cod_obs
print(dat, n = 2)
check_tam_data(dat)
```

Arrange your own data in the same four required tables. Catch and index contain
observations; weight and maturity contain biological inputs. Each index row
identifies its survey and sampling time as a fraction of the year. Optional
population covariates explain recruitment, cohort survival or natural mortality.
Catch-table covariates explain fishing mortality, while index-table covariates
explain catchability and index precision.

The example catches and indices use thousand fish, and weights use kg, giving
biomass in tonnes. Unit columns describe supplied values; they do not convert
them. Keep unavailable observations as `NA`. Genuine catch/index zeros remain in
the inputs but are excluded from the current lognormal likelihood. Biological
inputs must be complete. Read [input requirements](../reference/check_tam_data.html)
before fitting, and [the data help](../reference/cod_obs.html) for provenance.

## Specify three hypotheses

First fit a statistical catch-at-age model. Annual recruitment is estimated as
fixed effects, cohort survival follows the mortality calculation exactly, and F
is separable into annual and age effects. Natural mortality is supplied as 0.3
per year.

```{r scaa, cache=TRUE}
scaa <- fit_tam(
  dat, years = 1983:2025, ages = 2:14,
  N_settings = list(process = "off", init = "exp"),
  rec_settings = list(process = "off", mu_form = ~ factor(year)),
  F_settings = list(process = "off",
    mu_form = ~ factor(year) + factor(age), mean_ages = 5:14),
  M_settings = list(process = "off",
    mu_supplied = ~ I(0.3), mean_ages = 5:14),
  catch_settings = list(sd_form = ~ 1),
  index_settings = list(sd_form = ~ 1, q_form = ~ mono(q_block))
)
```

Age 14 is the modeled plus group: it includes older fish retained by the model's
biological calculations. `mean_ages` defines the ages used to report average
mortality. The catchability formula allows non-decreasing steps among `q_block`
groups under the default log link.

Now allow cohort-survival deviations, random-walk recruitment and correlated
annual F increments. This SAM-like model explains additional variation through
population processes while retaining the same observations and fixed M.

```{r sam, cache=TRUE, dependson="scaa"}
sam <- update(scaa,
  N_settings = list(process = "iid"),
  rec_settings = list(process = "rw", mu_form = NULL),
  F_settings = list(process = "cor_rw", mu_form = NULL)
)
```

The NCAM-like alternative keeps exact cohort survival but allows temporally
correlated F and M. Ages within each M block share actual M.

```{r ncam, cache=TRUE, dependson="scaa"}
ncam <- update(scaa,
  rec_settings = list(process = "rw", mu_form = NULL),
  F_settings = list(process = "ar1", mu_form = ~ 1),
  M_settings = list(process = "ar1", age_breaks = c(2, 5, 8, 14))
)
```

Partial updates retain omitted settings. These examples differ in several
deliberate assumptions; a focused investigation would also compare intermediate
models that change one assumption at a time. The [population equations](../reference/tinyAM-model.html)
describe process and initial-state conventions.

## Inspect diagnostics before trends

```{r checks}
check_tam(scaa, sam, ncam)
plot_model(scaa, sam, ncam)
```

`check_tam()` reports numerical checks separately from statistical advisories.
Convergence does not establish that the observations distinguish F, M and cohort
variation. Warnings and failed numerical checks are reasons to investigate, not
an invitation to rank the models immediately.

```{r dashboard, eval=FALSE}
vis_tam(scaa, sam, ncam, open_file = FALSE)
```

The dashboard opens with **Model structure**, including **Function calls**.
Start your diagnostic review in **Fisheries → Aggregate fishery** and **Surveys**:
inspect observed/predicted trajectories and residual patterns across age and
year. Retained OSA residuals are displayed when available; otherwise the plots
start with standardized residuals. Rendering never calculates OSAs implicitly.

Next inspect **Parameters** and **Tables → Diagnostics** for uncertainty and
process behavior. Then use **Trends** to compare abundance and mortality. The
pattern tabs show age–year structure; they can reveal differences hidden by
annual totals. Standardized residuals condition on fitted states and are affected
by shrinkage.

Public plotting functions reproduce these views outside the dashboard:

```{r ssb}
ssb <- get_ssb(SCAA = scaa, SAM = sam, NCAM = ncam)
plot_trend(ssb, color = ~model, colors = tam_pal(3),
           ylab = "SSB (tonnes)")
```

## Check historical stability and prediction

Withhold terminal years to examine retrospective change and predict the excluded
observations. Two folds keep this introduction small; use more for a substantive
comparison.

```{r hindcast, eval=FALSE}
hind <- fit_hindcast(scaa, sam, ncam, folds = 2)
hind
hind$fold_diagnostics
vis_tam(hind, model = "scaa", open_file = FALSE)
```

The printed summary includes Mohn's rho, survey log-RMSE, MASE and scored/failed
attempt counts. Rho describes retrospective change; values near zero indicate
greater historical stability. Lower log-RMSE indicates smaller log-scale forecast
errors. MASE below one beats keeping the last observed index value unchanged.

Default forecasts condition on the actual aggregate catch in the withheld year.
Survey observations and catch compositions remain held out. Agreement with the
imposed catch total therefore does not measure forecasting skill. Use
`proj_settings = list(F_mult = 1)` for a status-quo-F alternative.

Inspect failures and compare validation coverage before interpreting score
differences. Failed numerical fits are retained in diagnostics and excluded from
scores; unequal coverage is not a fair ranking. A few folds illustrate the
workflow without establishing which model is best. See [hindcast definitions](../reference/fit_retro.html)
for detailed scores and caller-controlled parallel execution.

For further comparisons, [AIC and cAIC](../reference/information_criteria.html)
have additional assumptions, especially for intrinsic random walks and
unpenalized initial states. They complement diagnostic and predictive checks.
